excerpts.text: Many upper-school science teachers are aware that last year (2019) a substantial revision to the SI unit system, commonly known in the US as the metric system, went into effect.
The revision completely changed the definitions of four of the seven SI base units and four of the important and related physical constants.
2. Four SI base units have been completely redefined:

3. mole—formerly defined as the amount of the substance that contained as many particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12, now defined as an amount of substance containing Avogadro’s number of particles, with Avogadro’s number given an exact value.

| *General Chemistry* *Chemistry for Accelerated Students* *Physics: Modeling Nature* | * Redefinition of the mole as simply the amount of substance containing Avogadro’s number of particles. * The average atomic mass of an atom in u (or Da) listed in the periodic table is no longer exactly equal to the molar mass in g/mol. However, it is close enough that the periodic table can still be used this way (relative difference of about 4 × 10–10) to determine molar masses of compounds. * Slight change to the value of Avogadro’s number, now equal to 6.02214076 × 1023. (The difference begins in the 7th digit.) * Reference data tables showing approximate values for *h*, *k*B, *e*, and *N*A. These are all exact now and the values are all slightly different from what they were before. * The gas constant, *R*, now has an exact value (since *R* = *k*B *N*A). * Comments about how the kilogram is defined in terms of an artifact. It no longer is. * A few exercises in the text include high enough precision that the new value for *N*A makes a difference in the last digit or two of the result. * Note that the unified atomic mass unit, u, also called the Dalton, Da, is still defined as exactly 1/12 the mass of an atom of carbon-12, and 1 u is still exactly equal to 1 Da. |
